title: Meet DESIGN.md: A new open standard for AI-generated UI
transcriptText:
DAVID EAST: DESIGN.md
is a text file
that describes a visual
identity and gives agents
a persistent and structured
understanding of a design
system.
Inside, it contains
everything that
defines how your design works--
things like the colors and what
they're for, the typography
and why you're using it,
and all the rules around
how it all fits together.
And when Stitch generates
new designs for your project,
this is the file
it reads to know
what design decisions to make.
And you can see
that on this canvas.
This DESIGN.md describes
Deep Midnight Forest Green
as the primary
ink for headlines.
And the headlines on the screen
are using that exact color.
It calls Track Terracotta
the accent for the buttons.
And that's the color
you see on the buttons.
And Stitch is using
all of this as context
for what it generates.
And that same context isn't
just useful inside of Stitch,
because other agents
can read this file.
And the use case for
DESIGN.md has been growing.
DESIGN.md files have been found
in IDEs and other agent tools,
and there's even
all these GitHub
repos and sites that curate
and share these design systems.
So we've put together
a DESIGN.md update.
We're introducing the first
draft of a specification
for the format.
This is a documented definition
of what a DESIGN.md actually
is and sets some ground rules.
So anyone who is reading
one or generating one all
is working from the same format.
And we've given
DESIGN.md a couple
new capabilities and a brand
new CLI to work with it.
To show you what I
mean, let's take a look
at a DESIGN.md in Antigravity.
A DESIGN.md has two kinds
of information in it.
There's the reasoning, like
why you chose the color
or what feeling you
wanted the font to carry.
And then there's
the actual values,
like the specific hex
codes and the font sizes.
And typically, these two
kinds of information, they
tend to live in separate places.
So you'll have a style guide
with all of the reasoning in it.
And then you'll have a config
file with all the tokens,
like a Tailwind config.
But over time, these two files
are going to drift apart.
So DESIGN.md now
introduces a Tokens section
that keeps both of this
information in the same file,
in context of one another.
So if you take a look
at this Color section,
it contains all
of the reasoning.
And this states that
the primary color
is the deep ink that's used
for the text and headlines.
And this is the reasoning.
So scrolling up to
the front matter,
the same value is
defined as a token.
And it's the same color that
we saw described in the prose.
But it's just expressed two
different ways inside the file.
And you'll see the same
pattern in other sections,
like Typography.
The prose describes what you
want the voice of the site
to feel like, and the
design token actually
describes the font
type and its size.
And obviously, this isn't
specific to one project.
Other DESIGN.md's follow
the same file structure,
even when the aesthetics
are completely different.
And when the agent
reads this file,
it's getting both types of
information, both the tokens
and the reasoning.
I've used the word
"token" a lot,
so let's dive in to
what it actually means.
Token isn't a
variable in the way
that we typically
think about variables.
It's more of a decision.
So when we say primary
is a color, it's true.
But it's more so primary
is a named decision.
Primary is a role in
this design system.
It is the main ink, the
text color of the page.
And the hex value is just what
fills that role at this time.
And the same idea shows up
in all these other sections
in DESIGN.md, like,
again, in typography.
Body main isn't
exactly a font size.
It's the role of a
default body copy.
And right now, it's
just decided that it's
Noto Serif at 18 pixels, and
that's what fills this role.
So the DESIGN.md spec makes
some baseline decisions,
but it's opened to extensions
and your own customizations.
And one of the baseline
decisions that it makes
is that everyone has to have
a primary color defined.
And in many design
systems, primary
is going to serve as the
primary color the user sees
on the page, which will be the
text and the ink, and neutral
will be the color that the
user is emotionally neutral to,
which is the canvas
or the surfaces,
really the background
of the page.
And when you start to think
about these colors as roles,
you'll actually start to design
a little differently because you
won't be trying to
match colors outright.
You'll be reaching for a
role that serves a purpose.
The DESIGN.md spec introduces
a whole bunch of sections,
and these are a lot of sections
that you're used to seeing.
And then, now,
these sections have
their own associated tokens.
But there is a new section
that we've been working on,
and it's still a
work in progress.
And we are very much wanting
feedback and contributions
on this.
And this section is Components.
Look at this button
primary token here.
It has a background color,
and it isn't a hex code.
It's actually a
reference to a color
that we've defined
in the front matter.
This component points at
a role that we defined
and it uses whatever
value lives there.
So when we update this role,
every component pointing to that
also follows along.
And right below, there
is another component
that works the same
way, a hover variant.
And it just overrides
one property,
which is the background color.
And it points at a different
variant of the same role
that we've already set up.
Components are a
work in progress,
but we're very excited
about their potential.
So please give us your
feedback, and help
us shape their direction.
In this update, we've
defined this Token section,
where you can define
these values that
live alongside the reasoning.
The biggest part of this update
isn't just the design tokens,
but it's the actual
specification
to DESIGN.md that we've
published the first draft to
on GitHub.
This GitHub repo holds
the spec and its rules,
but is also a place to file
issues, respond to comments,
and send in pull requests
for making contributions.
Anyone can read the spec
and bring their own feedback
and thinking back to us.
The main reason why we
have introduced DESIGN.md
as a specification is
that it has greatly
outgrown its original use.
There are so many tools
now that are generating
DESIGN.md's and other tools
that are consuming them,
and people are now using
them in so many ways
that we could have
never anticipated.
By establishing some core
rules for a specification,
everyone can work
from a common ground,
and there aren't just all
these different variations
and unexpected ways of
seeing DESIGN.md in the wild.
And we all can work from
the same foundation,
but at the same
time, still allowing
for extensions and
customizations that
fit any specific design system.
Effectively, we want to
provide a core set of rules
and structure that
everyone can rely on
while still providing a
whole space for flexibility
and creativity.
So how do agents and
other tools actually
work with a DESIGN.md spec?
Well, we've
introduced a CLI that
validates a DESIGN.md
against the actual spec.
So when an agent is
working with DESIGN.md,
it can actually
check its own work.
Here in Antigravity, I have
the same DESIGN.md open
with an agent in the side panel.
I'm going to ask it to add a new
accent button to the Components
section.
The agent makes this change.
It adds this button,
Accent Component,
with tertiary for the background
and primary for the text.
I'm going to ask this agent
to run the CLI to lint
against the file.
And the linter
catches something.
The pair the agent picked
has a contrast ratio issue,
and it's well below the
minimum that the WCAG requires
for body text.
And the agent now knows this,
and it can adjust this pair.
Or it can override
it if there is
a real reason for that choice.
And that's the loop
that the spec enables.
An agent reads the file's
context, makes a change,
and has a way to validate its
own work against the format.
The file isn't just
something that an agent just
consumes anymore.
It's something that an
agent can actually rely on.
Those are the core parts of
the update, a specification,
a new Tokens section, and
a CLI to check the work,
because the main
goal of this update
was to allow for DESIGN.md
to be easier to use outside
of Stitch and for everyone
to have a common ground
to work from.
If you want to try DESIGN.md,
start by generating one
in Stitch, and then check out
the specification, use the CLI,
and start using DESIGN.md
outside of Stitch
in other agents and other tools.
And if you're interested in
helping out with the spec,
providing feedback
or contribution,
please check out
the GitHub repo.
And we are very
excited to see what
you think of all of the
new updates in DESIGN.md.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
